When I opened the door, I could not believe what I saw. There was a small monkey sitting on our dining table, it was eating my sister's banana. I shouted and the monkey jumped onto the window. My mother came running from the kitchen with a broom.

The monkey looked at us and then it run away with the banana. We all start laughing. My sister was not happy because it was her banana, but I think it was the funniest thing that happend this year.

When I opened the door, I could not believe what I saw. Our living room, which my mother had cleaned that morning, was covered in feathers. Pillows lay torn open on the floor, and in the middle of the mess sat our puppy, Bruno, wagging his tail proudly.

I knew my mother would be home in ten minutes. Quickly, I grabbed a broom and started sweeping, but every time I made a pile, Bruno jumped into it and scattered the feathers again.

When my mother finally walked in, she stared at the room, then at me, and then at Bruno. To my surprise, she burst out laughing.

When I opened the door, I could not believe what I saw. My grandfather, who had not left his chair in months, was standing at the window, holding the curtain aside with one trembling hand.

"Look," he whispered. Outside, the neem tree he had planted forty years earlier was full of green parakeets, dozens of them, chattering as though they had come to deliver news.

I had walked past that tree every day without noticing it. Now, seeing it through his eyes, I understood why he had refused to let anyone cut it down. Some things, he once told me, are worth waiting for.

I think students should not use mobile phones at school. First, phones distract students from their lessons, many students play games instead of listening to the teacher. Second, some students may use phones to copy in tests. Also phones are expensive and they can be stolen or broken.

However, phones can be useful in emergency. Maybe students can keep their phones in the office and use it only when they need to call their parents. In conclusion, I believe phones should not be used in class.

Many people argue about whether students should be allowed to use mobile phones at school. In my opinion, phones should be allowed, but only with clear rules.

Phones can be powerful learning tools. Students can look up information, use dictionary apps and take photos of notes on the board. In an emergency, a phone also lets students contact their families quickly.

On the other hand, phones can be distracting, especially when students use social media during lessons. For this reason, schools should allow phones only at certain times, such as during research activities, and teachers should be able to collect them if they are misused.

Banning mobile phones in schools is tempting, but it treats a symptom rather than the cause. The real problem is not the device itself; it is that many students have never been taught to use it responsibly.

A total ban also ignores how much learning now happens online. A student researching a history project or practising pronunciation with a language app is using a phone exactly as a library card or a dictionary was once used.

Therefore, rather than banning phones, schools should teach digital self-discipline: phones stay silent and out of sight unless a teacher asks students to use them. Such a policy prepares students for adult life, where no one will confiscate their phones.
